title: Data Engineering: Pipelines, Warehouses and Lakehouses
description: How data moves from sources to analysis: pipelines, file and table formats, warehouses and lakehouses, batch and streaming processing, and running it all reliably.
audience: A capable adult who can query a table with SQL and read short Python programs (sql-from-rows-to-reports and python-for-data-analysis), preparing for work as a data engineer or for a certification such as Microsoft DP-700. No previous platform experience is assumed; named products are examples only.
outcomes: You'll be able to design a pipeline as a graph and make each step safe to rerun.
You'll be able to compare file formats, table formats and architectures by what a query must read.
You'll be able to work through partitions, shuffles, windows and watermarks with numbers.
You'll be able to decide how to check, monitor, secure and release a data pipeline.

modules.title: Moving data
modules.summary: What a pipeline is, the formats it carries, loading without duplicates, capturing changes and running the steps in order.

modules.title: Storing data
modules.summary: Warehouses, lakes and lakehouses, the open table formats that make files behave like tables, and how layout decides what a query reads.

modules.title: Processing data
modules.summary: Distributed batch processing, cleaning and deduplicating, and streaming with event time and watermarks.

modules.title: Running data platforms
modules.summary: Checking data as it moves, watching pipelines in production, and promoting and securing them across environments.

lessons.title: What a pipeline is
lessons.objective: Describe a pipeline as sources, steps and a sink arranged as a graph, tell batch from streaming and ETL from ELT, and name the property that makes a rerun safe.

concepts.title: Pipeline
concepts.summary: A pipeline is a set of steps that moves data from sources to a destination, with each step reading the output of the one before.

concepts.title: Batch and streaming
concepts.summary: Batch processes a bounded set of data on a schedule, while streaming processes an unbounded flow record by record or in small groups.

concepts.title: ETL and ELT
concepts.summary: ETL transforms data before loading it, ELT loads raw data first and transforms it inside the destination.

concepts.title: Idempotence
concepts.summary: A step is idempotent when running it twice leaves the destination in the same state as running it once.

misconceptions: Learners think pipelines are scripts that run once. In production they rerun, retry and backfill, so every step must tolerate a rerun.
Learners think streaming is just faster batch. It changes what data means: it never ends, arrives out of order, and results are updates.
Learners think ELT means no transformation. The transformation still happens, but inside the warehouse or lakehouse where the raw data sits.
sequence: Follow orders from a shop database to a sales dashboard: extract, land, clean, aggregate, serve.
Place the same flow on a spectrum from nightly batch through micro-batch to streaming.
Contrast ETL and ELT by where the cleaning code runs and what is kept.
Run an append step twice and watch the rows double; name the missing property.
examples: A nightly job that copies yesterday's orders is batch; a job that updates a fraud score as each card payment arrives is streaming.
An ELT pipeline lands raw JSON in a lakehouse bronze table and cleans it with SQL into silver; an ETL pipeline cleans in a separate engine first.
INSERT of 3 rows run twice into an empty table leaves 6 rows; an upsert on a key leaves 3.

figures.shows: A pipeline drawn as a directed graph: two sources, land, clean, join, aggregate, sink. Views: batch (boxes labelled with a schedule), streaming (a continuous flow), ETL and ELT (the transform box moves before or after the load).
figures.learnerAction: Switch views and drag a step to see which dependency arrows follow.

figures.shows: Stages of a worked order-to-dashboard flow in scrambled order.
figures.learnerAction: Place the stages in order.

questionPlan.sample: A card payment must have a fraud score within a second of arriving. Which processing style fits?
A step appends yesterday's rows to a table. Running it twice doubles the rows. Which property is missing? Give the one word.
Which description is ELT?
questionPlan.answer: Load raw files into the lakehouse first, then transform them with SQL there.
choices: Clean the data on a separate server, then load only the cleaned result.
Load raw files into the lakehouse first, then transform them with SQL there.
Transform data while it is being typed into the source.
Load the data and never transform it.

lessons.title: Files and formats
lessons.objective: Compare row-oriented and columnar formats, compute how many bytes a query must read from each, and explain what Parquet's row groups and footer statistics allow a reader to skip.

concepts.title: Row and column layout
concepts.summary: A row format stores each record together, while a columnar format stores each column together, which suits queries that read few columns of many rows.

concepts.title: Parquet structure
concepts.summary: A Parquet file holds row groups, each with a column chunk per column, and a footer with the schema and per-chunk statistics.

concepts.title: Encoding and compression
concepts.summary: Similar values stored together compress well, so a column of repeated values shrinks far more than the same values scattered across rows.

concepts.title: Schema in the file
concepts.summary: CSV carries no types and JSON carries names but not a fixed schema, while Parquet records column names and types in its footer.

misconceptions: Learners think file format is only about size. It decides which bytes a query must read at all.
Learners think CSV is fine because it opens in a spreadsheet. It has no types, ambiguous quoting and dates, and must be read in full.
Learners think columnar always wins. Fetching one whole record by key from a row store can be cheaper.
sequence: Take 100 million rows of 20 eight-byte columns and a query that needs two of them.
Show the same data as CSV rows and as column chunks.
Open a Parquet footer and read min and max for a column chunk.
Choose a format for archive, streaming messages, and analytics.
examples: 100,000,000 rows x 20 columns x 8 bytes is 16,000,000,000 bytes (16 GB); reading 2 columns from a columnar file is 1,600,000,000 bytes (1.6 GB) before compression.
A table of 50,000,000 rows read for 3 eight-byte columns is 1,200,000,000 bytes (1.2 GB).
A row group whose order_id column has min 1 and max 300 cannot contain order_id 500, so a filter on 500 skips it.

figures.shows: The same six-row, four-column table drawn two ways: stored row by row and stored column by column, with the bytes a two-column query touches shaded. Views: row layout, column layout, Parquet file with footer.
figures.learnerAction: Pick the columns a query needs and read the shaded byte count.

figures.shows: A format comparison table (CSV, JSON lines, Avro, Parquet) with rows for types, human-readable, splittable, columnar, typical use.
figures.learnerAction: Fill each cell by choosing.

questionPlan.sample: A table has 50,000,000 rows. A columnar query reads 3 columns of 8 bytes each. How many gigabytes (10^9 bytes) are read, ignoring compression?
A row-oriented file of 100,000,000 rows and 20 eight-byte columns must be read in full for a query that needs 2 columns. How many gigabytes (10^9 bytes) are read?
Which format best suits repeated analytical queries that read a few columns of billions of rows?

historyNotes: Parquet began as a joint effort of Twitter and Cloudera and became an Apache project in 2013. Confirm before printing.

lessons.title: Loading without duplicates
lessons.objective: Choose between full and incremental loads, use a watermark and an upsert, and predict the row count after a load is replayed.

concepts.title: Full and incremental loads
concepts.summary: A full load replaces the destination from the whole source, while an incremental load moves only rows that changed since the last run.

concepts.title: Watermark
concepts.summary: A stored high-water mark, such as the latest updated_at already loaded, marks where the next incremental run starts.

concepts.title: Upsert (merge)
concepts.summary: An upsert updates the row when its key exists and inserts it when it does not, so replaying a batch changes nothing.

concepts.title: Late-arriving rows
concepts.summary: A row committed at the source after the watermark has moved past its timestamp is skipped by a strict greater-than filter.

misconceptions: Learners think an incremental load is safe to rerun. A plain insert duplicates every row on retry; only a key-based upsert or overwrite of a partition is safe.
Learners set the watermark to the time the job ran. It must be the maximum change time actually seen in the data, since the clocks differ and rows commit late.
Learners use > on the watermark and never look back. Rows committed late with an older timestamp are lost, so many loads re-read a small overlap and rely on the upsert.
sequence: Load three customers, then replay a two-row batch with plain INSERT twice, then with an upsert.
Apply a watermark of 10:05 to four source rows with > and >=.
Show a row that arrives late and is missed.
Explain overwrite-by-partition as another idempotent pattern.
examples: A table of 3 rows plus a 2-row batch inserted twice without a key ends with 7 rows (4 distinct ids); the same batch as an upsert keyed on id ends with 4 rows after one or two runs.
Source updated_at values 10:03, 10:05, 10:06, 10:09 with watermark 10:05: > selects 2 rows, >= selects 3.
Target has max updated_at 2026-05-03; a source row with updated_at 2026-05-02 that committed late is never picked up by updated_at > max(updated_at).

figures.shows: Tables for a different example (products with id, price, updated_at) and an incoming batch, with an editable INSERT and upsert statement and the result after each run.
figures.learnerAction: Run the load once, run it again, and compare counts.

figures.shows: A time axis of source commits against the watermark line, with a late row appearing behind the line.
figures.learnerAction: Move the watermark and see which rows a > filter selects.

questionPlan.sample: Setup: CREATE TABLE customers(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT, updated_at TEXT); INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1,'a@x.com','2026-01-01'),(2,'b@x.com','2026-01-01'); Run this twice: INSERT INTO customers VALUES (2,'b2@x.com','2026-01-05'),(3,'c@x.com','2026-01-05') ON CONFLICT(id) DO UPDATE SET email=excluded.email, updated_at=excluded.updated_at; Then SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers. What is the count?
A table has 3 rows with ids 1, 2, 3. A 2-row batch (ids 2 and 4) is appended with a plain INSERT, no key, and the job is retried so the same batch is appended again. How many rows are in the table?
The previous run's watermark is 10:05. The source has rows updated at 10:03, 10:05, 10:06 and 10:09. How many rows does WHERE updated_at > '10:05' select?

lessons.title: Capturing changes
lessons.objective: Apply an ordered change log to a table and explain why log-based change capture sees deletes that a timestamp query cannot.

concepts.title: Change data capture
concepts.summary: CDC reads the source's change record, with an operation and a position for each insert, update and delete, instead of repeatedly querying the table.

concepts.title: Order by log position
concepts.summary: Changes must be applied in log order, because an update arriving before the insert it follows would be lost or misplaced.

concepts.title: Deletes
concepts.summary: A timestamp query cannot see a row that has gone, so deletes need the log, a soft-delete flag or a periodic key comparison.

concepts.title: Replicated copies
concepts.summary: A mirrored or replicated copy applies the log to keep a read-only analytic copy near-current without custom code.

misconceptions: Learners think updated_at finds every change. A hard delete leaves no row to carry a timestamp.
Learners apply changes in arrival order. Networks reorder; the log position, not arrival time, defines the order.
Learners think CDC is only a tool. It is an interface to the database's own record of what happened.
sequence: Compare polling a table with reading its log, using a delete as the test case.
Apply a log of inserts, updates and a delete to an empty table.
Reorder two entries and show the wrong result.
Name replicated and mirrored copies as managed CDC.
examples: Log in position order: (1) I id1 'a' (2) I id2 'b' (3) U id1 'a2' (4) D id2 (5) I id3 'c' (6) U id3 'c2' (7) U id1 'a3' (8) I id2 'b-new' leaves id1 'a3', id2 'b-new', id3 'c2': three rows.
If entry 4 (delete id2) were applied before entry 2 (insert id2) the table would wrongly end with 'b' for id2 before entry 8, which shows why order matters.
A source that hard-deletes row 2 shows no row 2 to an updated_at query, so the warehouse keeps the stale row.

figures.shows: A change-log table (position, operation, id, value) for a different log from the questions, beside a target table that updates as the learner steps through the log.
figures.learnerAction: Step the log and watch the target; drag two entries to reorder them.

figures.shows: Two arrows from a source: a polling query that misses a deleted row and a log reader that sees the delete. Views: polling, log.
figures.learnerAction: Delete a row at the source in each view.

questionPlan.sample: Apply this log in position order to an empty table: 1 I id1 'a'; 2 I id2 'b'; 3 U id1 'a2'; 4 D id2; 5 I id3 'c'; 6 U id3 'c2'; 7 U id1 'a3'; 8 I id2 'b-new'. What value does id1 hold at the end?
How many rows does the same table hold at the end?
Why does a nightly WHERE updated_at > watermark query not reflect rows hard-deleted at the source?
questionPlan.answer: A deleted row no longer exists to carry a timestamp.
choices: Deleted rows keep their old timestamp and are filtered out.
A deleted row no longer exists to carry a timestamp.
Timestamps are rewritten when a row is deleted.
The query is too slow to see deletes.

lessons.title: Orchestrating dependencies
lessons.objective: Read a pipeline as a directed acyclic graph, find its valid orders and critical path, and plan retries and a parallel backfill.

concepts.title: Directed acyclic graph
concepts.summary: Tasks are nodes and dependencies are arrows with no cycles, so there is always an order in which every task runs after its inputs.

concepts.title: Critical path
concepts.summary: The longest chain of dependent task durations sets the minimum time to finish, however many tasks run in parallel.

concepts.title: Retries and backoff
concepts.summary: A failed task is retried a limited number of times with growing waits, which only helps if the task is idempotent.

concepts.title: Backfill
concepts.summary: Re-running a pipeline for past periods works by giving each run its own period as a parameter, in parallel up to a limit.

misconceptions: Learners think more workers always shortens a run. The critical path is a floor.
Learners hard-code today's date inside a task. A rerun for yesterday then produces today's data; the period must be a parameter.
Learners retry everything. Retrying a non-idempotent step multiplies side effects.
sequence: A five-task graph with durations A 5, B 10, C 4, D 6, E 2 minutes.
Count the valid orders and find the longest path.
Retry waits of 2, 4 and 8 minutes.
Backfill 30 daily partitions at 4 in parallel.
examples: A (5 min) feeds B (10) and C (4); both feed D (6); D feeds E (2). The critical path A, B, D, E takes 5+10+6+2 = 23 minutes against 27 minutes of total work.
There are 2 valid orders: A, B, C, D, E and A, C, B, D, E.
Thirty daily partitions, each run taking 12 minutes, 4 at a time: ceil(30/4) = 8 waves x 12 = 96 minutes.

figures.shows: A different five-task graph (not the one in the questions) with durations on the nodes, a Gantt strip below showing the schedule, and a worker-count slider. Views: graph, schedule.
figures.learnerAction: Change the worker count and read the finish time.

figures.shows: A different seven-task graph, with the learner choosing a valid run order.
figures.learnerAction: Drag tasks into a valid order.

questionPlan.sample: Task A (5 min) feeds B (10) and C (4). B and C both feed D (6). D feeds E (2). With unlimited workers, what is the minimum total time in minutes?
How many different valid run orders does that graph have?

lessons.title: Warehouses, lakes and lakehouses
lessons.objective: Choose between a warehouse, a lake and a lakehouse for a given need, and explain schema-on-write versus schema-on-read and the medallion layers.

concepts.title: Warehouse
concepts.summary: A warehouse stores structured, modelled data under a schema it enforces on write, and serves SQL analytics with strong consistency.

concepts.title: Data lake
concepts.summary: A lake keeps files of any kind in cheap object storage with structure applied when they are read.

concepts.title: Lakehouse
concepts.summary: A lakehouse puts a table format and transactions over lake files so one copy serves both engineering and SQL analytics.

concepts.title: Medallion layers
concepts.summary: Bronze holds data as received, silver holds cleaned and conformed data, and gold holds business-ready aggregates.

misconceptions: Learners think a lake is a dumping ground that needs no design. Without structure, ownership and tables it becomes unusable.
Learners think warehouse and lakehouse are rivals. They share engines and formats, and many platforms use both.
Learners think the medallion layers are three copies for their own sake. Each layer has a different contract with its consumers.
sequence: Describe the same orders data as a warehouse table, a folder of JSON, and a Delta table.
Separate storage from compute, and show why that lets several engines read one copy.
Walk raw JSON through bronze, silver and gold.
Place four requests (raw audit copy, cleaned customers, monthly revenue, ad hoc ML features) in a layer.
examples: Raw JSON events land in bronze unchanged, silver holds one row per event with typed columns and duplicates removed, and gold holds revenue per day per region.
In Microsoft Fabric a lakehouse and a warehouse can read the same Delta files in OneLake; Databricks offers a comparable pairing (examples, not requirements).
A schema-on-write system rejects a row with a text value in a numeric column at load time; a schema-on-read system accepts the file and fails at query time.

figures.shows: Three architectures side by side: warehouse (data and engine together), lake (files plus engines), lakehouse (files plus table format plus engines). Views: architecture, a query path, medallion layers.
figures.learnerAction: Pick an architecture and trace a query from the file to the result.

figures.shows: Five requests with a choice of layer or architecture.
figures.learnerAction: Match each request to its best place.

questionPlan.sample: Which system applies a schema when data is read rather than when it is written?
A table holds one cleaned row per customer, with types fixed and duplicates removed. Which medallion layer is it?
Several engines (SQL and Spark) must read the same single copy of the data with transactions. Which architecture fits?

historyNotes: James Dixon, then at Pentaho, is usually credited with the term data lake in 2010, and the lakehouse term was popularised by Databricks around 2020. Confirm before printing.

lessons.title: Open table formats
lessons.objective: Read a Delta or Iceberg commit history to find which files make up a table at any version, and explain how optimistic commits give readers a consistent snapshot.

concepts.title: Transaction log
concepts.summary: A table format records each commit as a list of files added and removed, and a table is the set of files not yet removed at a chosen version.

concepts.title: Snapshots and atomic commit
concepts.summary: A commit becomes visible all at once, so a reader sees a complete earlier version or a complete later one, never half of a write.

concepts.title: Time travel
concepts.summary: Because old versions are recorded, a query can read the table as of a version or time until the old files are removed.

concepts.title: Compaction and vacuum
concepts.summary: Compaction rewrites many small files into fewer large ones, and vacuum deletes files no longer referenced after a retention period.

misconceptions: Learners think a table format is a database. It is metadata over immutable files, and the engines do the work.
Learners think deleting rows removes data immediately. The commit marks files as removed; the bytes stay until vacuum.
Learners think concurrent writers lock the table. Writers commit optimistically and one retries if they conflict.
sequence: Replay five commits and list the live files at each version.
Read a checkpoint plus the commits after it.
Draw the Iceberg chain from catalog pointer to metadata file, manifest list, manifest and data file.
Run a compaction and a vacuum and count the files.
examples: Delta commit files are named by version, zero-padded to 20 digits, such as 00000000000000000012.json.
Commits: v0 adds a, b; v1 adds c; v2 removes a and adds d; v3 adds e and removes b; v4 removes c and d and adds f (a compaction). The table at v2 is {b, c, d}, at v3 {c, d, e}, and at v4 {e, f}.
After v4, six files exist on storage (a to f) but only two are in the current table until a vacuum deletes the rest.

figures.shows: A commit history strip for a different table history from the questions, with a file ledger below showing added and removed files, and a version slider. Views: Delta log, Iceberg metadata tree.
figures.learnerAction: Slide to a version and read the live file set.

figures.shows: The Iceberg read path (catalog pointer, metadata file, manifest list, manifest, data file) in scrambled order.
figures.learnerAction: Place the layers in order.

questionPlan.sample: Commits: v0 adds a, b. v1 adds c. v2 removes a and adds d. v3 adds e and removes b. v4 removes c and d and adds f. How many data files are in the table at version 3?

lessons.title: Partitioning and file layout
lessons.objective: Estimate how much data a filtered query reads under a partitioning scheme, pick a partition column of the right cardinality and explain the small-files problem.

concepts.title: Partition pruning
concepts.summary: When data is split into directories by a column, a filter on that column lets the engine skip every other directory.

concepts.title: Partition cardinality
concepts.summary: A partition column needs a modest number of distinct values, because tens of thousands of tiny partitions cost more to list than they save.

concepts.title: Small files
concepts.summary: Many small files add per-file overhead for listing, opening and metadata, so writers target files of hundreds of megabytes.

concepts.title: Data skipping
concepts.summary: Per-file minimum and maximum statistics let an engine skip files whose range cannot match a filter, and clustering sorts data so the ranges are tight.

misconceptions: Learners partition by the column they filter on most, whatever its cardinality. A column with millions of values creates millions of tiny files.
Learners think partitioning speeds every query. A query that does not filter on the partition column reads everything.
Learners think min/max statistics always skip. Random order makes every file's range overlap, so none can be skipped.
sequence: A 730 GB table partitioned into 365 equal daily partitions and a one-week filter.
The same table partitioned by customer id across 2 million customers.
Four files with min/max ranges and a point filter.
Compaction and clustering as the repair.
examples: 730 GB over 365 daily partitions is 2 GB per partition; a 7-day filter reads 14 GB, which is 1.92% of the table.
730 GB across 2,000,000 customer partitions is 365,000 bytes (365 KB) per partition, far too small to read efficiently.
Files with order_id ranges F1 [1,300], F2 [250,600], F3 [601,900], F4 [400,700]: a filter order_id = 500 cannot skip F2 or F4, so 2 files are read.

figures.shows: A bar chart of partition sizes for date versus customer-id partitioning, with a threshold line for a healthy file size.
figures.learnerAction: Switch the partition column and see sizes and file counts.

figures.shows: Four file range bars on a number line, with ranges different from the questions, and a movable filter line, showing which files are skipped.
figures.learnerAction: Move the filter and count the files that remain.

questionPlan.sample: A 730 GB table has 365 equal daily partitions. A query filters 7 days. How many gigabytes does it read?

lessons.title: Distributed processing
lessons.objective: Reason about partitions, tasks, narrow and wide transformations and shuffles, and explain why one skewed key can set the run time of a whole stage.

concepts.title: Partitions and tasks
concepts.summary: A distributed engine splits data into partitions and runs one task per partition, in waves limited by the number of cores.

concepts.title: Narrow and wide transformations
concepts.summary: Narrow steps such as filter and map work within each partition, while wide steps such as group by and join move rows between partitions in a shuffle.

concepts.title: Lazy evaluation
concepts.summary: Transformations only build a plan, and an action such as count or write triggers the work, which lets the engine optimise the plan first.

concepts.title: Skew and broadcast
concepts.summary: A key holding most of the rows makes one task far slower than the rest, and joining a small table can avoid a shuffle by sending it to every executor.

misconceptions: Learners think adding machines speeds up everything. A shuffle moves data across the network and a skewed key keeps one task busy.
Learners think each line of code runs when written. Transformations are lazy; the work happens at the action.
Learners think a join is always a shuffle. A small table can be broadcast, avoiding the shuffle.
sequence: Count tasks: 10 GiB of input in 128 MiB splits.
Waves: 80 tasks on 20 cores.
Shuffle blocks: 80 map tasks to 200 reduce partitions.
A hot key with 60% of 1,000 million rows across 10 reducers.
Broadcast a 50 MB table instead of shuffling 2 TB.
examples: 10 GiB is 10,240 MiB; in 128 MiB splits that is 80 partitions and so 80 tasks; on 20 cores they run in 4 waves.
80 map tasks writing to 200 reduce partitions can produce 80 x 200 = 16,000 shuffle blocks.

With 1,000 million rows, 10 reducers, one key holding 60% and a rate of 1 million rows per second per task, the hot task needs 600 s while a perfectly even split needs 100 s, and the stage ends at 600 s.

lessons.title: Cleaning and deduplicating
lessons.objective: Write the SQL that keeps the latest record per key, cast and trim columns safely, and explain why deduplication must come before aggregation.

concepts.title: Keep the latest per key
concepts.summary: ROW_NUMBER over a partition by the key, ordered by load time descending, then keeping row 1, removes duplicates and keeps the newest record.

concepts.title: Typing and trimming
concepts.summary: Raw text is trimmed and cast to its true type in the silver step, and values that cannot be cast become explicit nulls or rejects.

concepts.title: Order of steps
concepts.summary: Deduplicate before aggregating, because a sum over duplicated rows counts the same event more than once.

concepts.title: Rejects
concepts.summary: Rows that fail typing go to a rejects table with the reason, so nothing disappears silently.

misconceptions: Learners dedupe with SELECT DISTINCT. It only removes rows identical in every column, so a re-sent record with a new load time survives.
Learners aggregate first and clean later. The totals are already wrong.
Learners drop bad rows quietly. A reject table keeps the evidence and the count.
sequence: A bronze table with repeated event ids and padded amounts.
Rank rows per event_id by loaded_at descending and keep rank 1.
Sum before and after deduplication and compare.
Send non-numeric amounts to rejects with the reason.
examples: Bronze rows: e1 ' 10.50' (loaded 03-01), e1 '10.50' (03-02), e2 '7', e3 'x' (03-01), e3 '4' (03-02), e4 '5'. Keeping the latest per event gives e1 10.5, e2 7, e3 4 and e4 5, a total of 26.5.
Summing every bronze row after casting (non-numeric 'x' counts as 0 in SQLite) gives 37.0, which overstates the truth by 10.5.
DISTINCT on all columns would keep both e1 rows because loaded_at differs.

figures.shows: A different bronze table (sensor readings with duplicates), the ranked table with a rn column, and the result after keeping rn = 1.
figures.learnerAction: Edit the ORDER BY direction and see which rows survive.

lessons.title: Streaming and event time
lessons.objective: Assign events to tumbling, sliding and session windows, compute a watermark, and explain what at-least-once delivery means for an idempotent sink.

concepts.title: Event time and processing time
concepts.summary: Event time is when something happened, processing time is when the system saw it, and the gap between them is lateness.

concepts.title: Windows
concepts.summary: A tumbling window is fixed and non-overlapping, a sliding window overlaps when its slide is shorter than its length, and a session window closes after a gap with no events.

concepts.title: Watermark
concepts.summary: The watermark is the maximum event time seen minus the allowed lateness, and windows ending before it are finalised and their state dropped.

concepts.title: Delivery guarantees
concepts.summary: With at-least-once delivery a failure replays records, so a sink that is idempotent or deduplicates by key makes the result effectively exactly once.

misconceptions: Learners window by arrival time. Results then change with network delay; windows should use event time.
Learners think a watermark drops every late event at once. It only lets the engine finalise state; the engine does not guarantee dropping data later than the threshold.
Learners expect exactly-once for free. The sources replay after failure, so the sink must tolerate duplicates.
sequence: Events at 10:01, 10:04, 10:06, 10:09, 10:10 into 5-minute tumbling windows.
A 10-minute window sliding every 5 minutes: each event falls in two windows.
Session windows with a 5-minute gap over minutes 0, 2, 3, 10, 12, 20.
Maximum event time 10:42 with 10 minutes of allowed lateness.
A consumer that committed offset 120 and processed 10 more records before a crash.
examples: A 10-minute window sliding every 5 minutes puts each event in 10/5 = 2 windows; the sessions over minutes 0, 2, 3, 10, 12, 20 with a 5-minute gap are {0,2,3}, {10,12}, {20}: 3 sessions.

Max event time 10:42 minus 10 minutes lateness gives watermark 10:32, so the window [10:20,10:30) is closed; a consumer that committed offset 120 and processed offsets 120 to 129 before crashing reprocesses 10 records after restart.

lessons.title: Checking data in motion
lessons.objective: Place validation gates in a pipeline, classify a schema change as safe or breaking, and decide whether a batch passes a rejection threshold.

concepts.title: Validation gate
concepts.summary: A gate checks schema, ranges and keys at a layer boundary and decides to pass, quarantine or stop the run.

concepts.title: Schema evolution
concepts.summary: Adding a nullable column is usually safe, while removing, renaming or retyping a column breaks readers.

concepts.title: Quarantine and dead letters
concepts.summary: Failing rows are written aside with the reason, so good rows continue and bad rows can be fixed and replayed.

concepts.title: Fail fast on drift
concepts.summary: If a source changes shape unexpectedly, stopping the run loudly is better than loading wrong data quietly.

misconceptions: Learners treat any new column as harmless. A column that changes a join key or a meaning is breaking even if it is added.
Learners let the pipeline auto-adapt to any schema. Silent adaptation moves a source bug into every downstream table.
Learners discard failing rows. Without a quarantine there is no count and no way to repair.
sequence: Five schema changes to classify: add nullable column, drop column, rename column, widen int to bigint, change string to int.
A batch of 1,000 rows with 30 null keys against a 2% threshold.
A gate that quarantines rows and one that stops the run.
Where gates sit: landing, bronze to silver, silver to gold.
examples: Adding a nullable column is safe; dropping or renaming a column breaks readers; changing string to int breaks parsers.
30 failing rows of 1,000 is 3%, which exceeds a 2% threshold, so the run stops and alerts instead of publishing.
A gate that finds 5 of 1,000 rows failing (0.5%) quarantines them and lets the other 995 continue.

lessons.title: Monitoring and tuning
lessons.objective: Compute throughput and freshness against a service target, and diagnose a slow or failing job from its symptoms.

concepts.title: Freshness
concepts.summary: Freshness is the age of the newest data in a table, checked against a target such as under six hours.

concepts.title: Throughput and latency
concepts.summary: Throughput is rows or bytes per second, and latency is the time from arrival to availability.

concepts.title: Run signals
concepts.summary: Duration, rows in and out, retries and failures per run reveal problems before users do.

concepts.title: Common slow causes
concepts.summary: Skew, too many small files, unneeded shuffles, reading unneeded columns and under-sized capacity cause most slow jobs.

misconceptions: Learners monitor only failures. A job that succeeds with half the usual rows is also broken.
Learners tune by adding capacity first. Layout and skew fixes are cheaper and last.
Learners measure the schedule, not the data. The pipeline can run on time and still publish stale data.
sequence: A table last loaded at 02:10 with a six-hour target checked at 09:00.
A job moving 90 million rows in 30 minutes.
Match symptoms (one task far slower, thousands of tiny files, a full scan with a filter) to causes.
Name the four signals worth alerting on.
examples: Checked at 09:00, a table last loaded at 02:10 is 6 h 50 min old; against a 6-hour target it is 50 minutes late.
90,000,000 rows in 30 minutes (1,800 seconds) is 50,000 rows per second.
One task running far longer than its siblings suggests skew; thousands of tiny files suggest a compaction problem.

lessons.title: Environments, security and release
lessons.objective: Explain how a pipeline moves from development to production under version control, and choose the access control that fits a data-protection need.

concepts.title: Environments
concepts.summary: Development, test and production are separate places with the same structure, and a release promotes tested changes rather than editing production.

concepts.title: Version control and deployment
concepts.summary: Pipeline definitions live in a repository, and an automated deployment applies them to each environment with environment-specific parameters.

concepts.title: Access control
concepts.summary: Roles grant access to workspaces and items, and finer controls restrict rows, columns or files to the people who need them.

concepts.title: Secrets and identities
concepts.summary: Credentials are held in a secret store and used by service identities, never written into code or notebooks.

misconceptions: Learners edit production directly to fix a bug quickly. That bypasses testing and leaves no history.
Learners give everyone workspace admin to avoid access problems. Least privilege limits the harm of a mistake or a stolen account.
Learners copy connection strings into notebooks. Anyone with the notebook then holds the credential.
sequence: Trace a change from a branch to dev, test and production, with parameters for each connection.
Row-level security: a regional manager sees only their region's rows.
Column-level security or masking: analysts see a masked email.
Move a password from a notebook to a secret store.
examples: A change merged to main deploys to test, where the pipeline runs on a sample, then is promoted to production with production connection parameters.
A regional sales manager who may only see EMEA rows needs row-level security; an analyst who may see orders but not emails needs column-level security or masking.
In Microsoft Fabric, deployment pipelines and Git integration cover promotion and version control; other platforms use their own CI/CD (an example, not a requirement).
